source.title: Neural Data Transformer 2: Multi-context Pretraining for Neural Spiking Activity
source.authors: Joel Ye; J. Collinger; Leila Wehbe; Robert A. Gaunt

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or cutoff; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling of pretraining data in a new setting—neural spiking activity—and reports supervised decoding and unsupervised reconstruction outcomes. It does not test language-model scaling directly.
record.gate_note: The scaling experiments vary pretraining data volume and target-session calibration data, not model parameters or training compute. No power-law fit, exponent, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is reported. Figure 4 values are not given numerically in the text, so the plotted values are recorded as figure only.
record.test_reason: The study scales pretraining data for a masked-autoencoder Transformer on neural spiking activity, a new modality. It reports held-out reconstruction NLL and downstream decoding R² as data grows. It fits no power law, varies neither parameters nor compute, and gives plotted values only in figures, so it bears on V5 and V6 only qualitatively.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that broad pretraining, even at 10-100K trials, helps neural spiking models and practical decoding. They find distinct scaling slopes per context class, contrasting with the constant offset in Kaplan et al. Unsupervised reconstruction gains appear very limited, and the authors say extrapolating beyond the explored scale is difficult.
record.recipe_differences: Uses masked-autoencoder Transformer pretraining on neural spiking activity and scales data volume; it does not use the language-model loss, parameter/token/compute sweeps, power-law fitting, or compute-optimal allocation methods in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling slopes and benefits vary by pretraining context class (cross-session, cross-subject, cross-task). The paper notes masking ratio may affect scaling trends but says compute limits prevented assessing this.

fits_no_version.finding: In human offline decoding, adding monkey data to pretraining or decoder preparation lowers R² (e.g. P2 0.503 vs 0.443-0.490).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding more but cross-species pretraining data can reduce downstream performance; scale benefits depend on data relevance.

record.problems: The tested scale is modest (largest pretraining data on the order of 100K trials); model size is held relatively static, with no power-law fits or extrapolation test. Hyperparameters were not broadly swept, and scaling analysis is limited to selected neural-data contexts. Several plotted values are not supplied numerically in the text.

untested.parts: Power-law functional form and exponents. Scaling in parameters or compute (model size held roughly static at 6-12 layers). Image/video and repeated-data regimes.
Language-model downstream tasks. A quantitative mapping from pretraining loss to downstream performance. Predictive extrapolation.
Not tested: no fit-and-extrapolate. The authors say extrapolation beyond the explored scale is difficult.
Not tested: no fixed-compute allocation sweep.
Not tested: no shape comparison at fixed parameter count (only patch-size and design ablations).
Not tested for fitted exponents. Different slopes across data sources are noted but not fitted.

missing.what: In-distribution from-scratch scaling curve: single-session NLL/R² vs intra-session trials. This is the comparison baseline; the single-session model reaches the lowest NLL.
Replication of all three scaling analyses on the first and final evaluation sessions, with the same conclusions.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not a scaling-law paper: it fits no power law, and pretraining spans only about two orders of magnitude beyond the largest single-context models. Links to V6 are loose because the system is not a language model. The model was held near 3M parameters; the authors say larger models gave no return, but report no numbers.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out cross-entropy results or power-law fits over parameters, tokens, or compute.
The study says scaling trends may forecast larger-data utility, but does not fit on small runs and predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep over parameter and token allocation.
No comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.

Tests scaling with neural-data pretraining volume, but does not fit or establish a power-law form. It does not test image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer as distinct training regimes.
Tests downstream neural decoding performance against pretraining-data scale; does not test language-model downstream tasks or a quantitative mapping from pretraining loss to downstream performance.
Reports differing scaling slopes across neural-data context classes, but does not test fitted language-model exponents, compute-optimal allocations, parameter counting, or fitting-method dependence.

statements.correction: Cross-session decoding scaling starts to saturate; cross-subject and cross-task slopes are shallower. The largest task-pretrained model matches approximately 800 single-session trials in decoding and 300 in NLL. V6 label: limits_scope.
statements.problem: The NDT2 description is accurate, but the challenges label overstates these results: decoding improves, with saturation and source-dependent slopes rather than an absent or reversed effect.
